summary: Defines the PLAIN SASL mechanism, a simple clear-text user and password method for use together with confidentiality from a lower layer such as TLS in protocols that lack a simple password command. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: You tell the guard your name and password. It is simple but safe only if no one can overhear, so it is used inside a secret tunnel.

subtitle: A one-message username and password login for SASL, safe only when the connection is already encrypted.

tldr.problem: Some protocols have no simple command for logging in with a user name and password, but still need one that works with existing password databases.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a single UTF-8 message holding an optional authorization identity, the authentication identity and the clear-text password, separated by NUL characters. The server checks them against its authentication database.
tldr.outcome: PLAIN gives no integrity or confidentiality itself, so it is meant to run under TLS. Servers by default should not offer it without adequate data security.

facts.label: Message parts
facts.value: authzid, authcid and passwd, separated by NUL

today: RFC 4616 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8996. It updates RFC 2595, replacing its Section 6.

sections.title: Why a Plain Password Mechanism
sections.content:
Clear-text, multiple-use passwords are simple and work with almost all existing operating system authentication databases. They also help with a smooth move to a more secure password-based mechanism. The drawback is that they are unacceptable on network connections where data confidentiality is not ensured.

PLAIN is a SASL mechanism for protocols that have no clear-text login command, such as ACAP or SMTP-AUTH. It provides no security layer. It replaces Section 6 of RFC 2595.
sections.eli5: Some programs have no easy way to log in with a name and password. PLAIN gives them one, as long as the line is kept private.

sections.title: The PLAIN Message
sections.content:
The mechanism is a single message from client to server: a string of UTF-8 encoded Unicode characters. It holds the authorization identity (who to act as), a NUL (U+0000) character, the authentication identity (whose password is used), another NUL, and the clear-text password.

The grammar is message = [authzid] UTF8NUL authcid UTF8NUL passwd. Each of the three parts is one or more non-NUL UTF-8 characters, and servers MUST accept each up to and including 255 octets. A UTF-8 character can be up to 4 octets. If the client leaves out the authorization identity, the server derives one from the credentials.

The form of authzid depends on the application protocol's SASL profile. The authcid and passwd are form-free, and non-visible characters or ones a user may be unable to type are discouraged.
sections.eli5: The login is one note with three parts: who you want to be, who you are, and your secret word. Little invisible dividers keep them apart.

sections.title: How the Server Verifies It
sections.content:
On receiving the message, the server checks the authentication identity and password against its authentication database. It also checks that those credentials permit the client to act as the presented or derived authorization identity. If both succeed, the user is authenticated.

Strings should be prepared before comparison. The SASLprep profile of StringPrep is RECOMMENDED but not mandatory, so a server can use another algorithm, or none, for example to interoperate with an external system. Presented strings are treated as query strings, so unassigned code points are allowed. Database strings are treated as stored strings, so unassigned code points are prohibited.

If the server stores the output of a non-invertible function such as a hash, the string MUST be prepared before it goes into that function. If preparation fails or gives an empty string, verification SHALL fail. With no authorization identity given, the server derives one from the prepared authentication identity. The server MAY also use the credentials to initialize another authentication database, such as one for CRAM-MD5 or DIGEST-MD5.

The RFC also gives non-definitive pseudo-code for a Verify function that prepares the identity and password, fetches the stored hash, compares it, derives the authorization identity if needed, and calls Authorize.
sections.eli5: The server cleans up what you typed, looks you up, checks the password, and checks that you are allowed to act as who you asked for. Any failed step means no entry.

sections.title: Example Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC shows two non-definitive examples using ACAP. In the first, the client starts TLS, sees that the server now offers PLAIN, sends AUTHENTICATE "PLAIN", and then the message <NUL>tim<NUL>tanstaaftanstaaf (an empty authorization identity). The server answers OK.

In the second, the client sends Ursel<NUL>Kurt<NUL>xipj3plmq as an initial response, which saves a round trip. It asks to act as Ursel using Kurt's credentials, and the server refuses with NO because that authorization identity is not permitted.
sections.eli5: In one example someone logs in as themselves and gets in. In the other, someone tries to act as another person and is turned away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PLAIN gives no integrity or confidentiality protection, so it should not be used without adequate external protection such as TLS. By default, implementations SHOULD NOT advertise and SHOULD NOT use it unless adequate data security services are in place.

Even under TLS, the server learns the password, so it gains the ability to impersonate the user to all services with the same password. Clients are encouraged to have an operational mode where all mechanisms likely to reveal the password to the server are disabled. General SASL, Unicode, UTF-8 and StringPrep security considerations also apply.

IETF specifications that name PLAIN as an applicable mechanism MUST mandate support for a strong data security service, such as TLS.
sections.eli5: If someone is listening, they hear your password. Even the person you tell it to could reuse it elsewhere, so only use it in a private room and with someone you trust.

viz.caption: ABNF FOR THE PLAIN CLIENT MESSAGE (RFC 4616)

data.title: PLAIN message grammar
data.code:
message   = [authzid] UTF8NUL authcid UTF8NUL passwd
authcid   = 1*SAFE ; MUST accept up to 255 octets
authzid   = 1*SAFE ; MUST accept up to 255 octets
passwd    = 1*SAFE ; MUST accept up to 255 octets
UTF8NUL   = %x00 ; UTF-8 encoded NUL character
